sentences.text: The genus exhibits traits of both long-tailed and short-tailed pterosaurs and is described as a transitional fossil between these two groups.
In all species, the teeth were widely spaced, spike-like, and set in sockets with raised margins, with the longest teeth located at the jaw tips.
Specimens are divided into four distinct species, primarily distinguished by the size and shape of their teeth.
Unlike other wukongopterids, the male head crest was supported by a thin bony skull extension with a serrated edge, likely to anchor a larger keratinous crest.
The genus exhibited sexual dimorphism, with females lacking a crest and having wider hips than males.
Darwinopterus was likely a saltatorial insectivore that hopped through trees and on the ground, similar to modern songbirds.
Researchers suggest the robust teeth of D. robustodens were adapted for feeding on hard-shelled beetles.
Numerous well-preserved specimens, including an egg, have allowed researchers to deduce Darwinopterus biology, such as growth patterns, life history, reproduction, and potential sexual variation.
Darwinopterus eggs had a parchment-like, soft shell, similar to those of later pterosaurs and modern reptiles.
Darwinopterus eggs weighed about 6 grams when laid but could double in weight due to moisture absorption by the time of hatching.
The type species, Darwinopterus modularis, was first described in February 2010.
The genus Darwinopterus was described by Lü and colleagues in 2009.
The holotype specimen ZMNH M8782 is fairly well-preserved but lacks important parts of some limbs.
In 2015, the "Mrs T" specimen was reassigned to the genus Kunpengopterus, and in 2021 it was classified as the species Kunpengopterus antipollicatus.
David Unwin suggested that Darwinopterus likely laid many small eggs that were buried, and that juveniles could fly immediately upon hatching with little to no parental care.
A 2015 report of the specimen's counterplate revealed a second egg in the body, indicating that Darwinopterus had two active ovaries, each producing one egg at a time.
Darwinopterus belongs to the family Wukongopteridae.
Between 30 and 40 fossil specimens of Darwinopterus were found in the Tiaojishan Formation, dating to the Middle Jurassic period approximately 160.89 to 160.25 million years ago.
Fossil occurrences of Darwinopterus date from the Bathonian to the Kimmeridgian stages, between 168.2 and 152.21 million years ago.
In 2024, it was suggested that the genus Darwinopterus is polyphyletic, with phylogenetic analyses placing the other three species in various positions rather than as a single group.

The hypothesis of sexual dimorphism in Darwinopterus has been criticized; researcher Kevin Padian suggested that crest size and shape may change with age, similar to ceratopsian dinosaurs, rather than indicating sex.
While originally described as a raptorial hawking carnivore, later analyses found no evidence supporting aerial predation.
